title: The if Statement
learning_outcomes: Explain what the if statement contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: basic conditions.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Control flow chooses which statements run and how many times. Every branch should cover the intended cases, and each loop should have a clear update and termination condition. In this lesson, focus on basic conditions; then compare it with if and else. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use the if statement when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Control flow chooses which statements run and how many times. Every branch should cover the intended cases, and each loop should have a clear update and termination condition. For the if statement, begin with basic conditions. Also distinguish if and else; elseif; nested conditions. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for the if statement from top to bottom. Start by identifying basic conditions, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
